title: About the Instructor
text:
I am Paulo Fagandini, and I will be the instructor of this course. I have a doctorate in Economics from Nova School of Business and Economics, where I did my dissertation on Applied Microeconomic Theory, working in Contracts, Matching, and Auctions.
After that I did a postdoc in Corporate Finance at Nova Finance Center, where I worked doing empirical research.
Nowadays, I currently teach Mathematics at the doctoral and master level at Nova SBE, and Microeconomics and Statistics at the Polytechnic University of Lisbon. I also teach Economics at the Universidade Europeia, also in Lisbon.
I have published articles in journals like Managerial and Decision Economics, and Computational Economics, chapters on peer reviewed books, and I worked recently as co-editor in a book about agent based models. I have done peer reviews for several scientific publications.

The course has as its main goal to help students understand how incentives shape behavior in organizations of different kinds, and confront them with several situations where the economic theory provides a useful framework to implement solutions to these issues.
By the end of the course, it is expected that students will be able to apply basic game-theoretic and contract-theoretic models to analyze strategic situations, and furthermore, to recognize incentive problems in organizations and public policy settings.

Rules of the Game
For any game we want to model, we will need to define some components:

who is playing. (players)
what are they playing with. (actions, strategies)
when each player gest to play.
how much they can gain or lose. (payoffs)
Further, we assume players are equally informed about these rules.

title: Introduction:  Incentives Matter

Strategic form
When using the strategic form, we represent a game with a table, where rows and columns represent strategies for each player. The cells in the table will contain the payoffs. Because convention, we place the first player on the left, with her strategies in rows, and the second player on top, with her strategies represented in the columns.
Payoffs will be represented again as an ordered pair, where the first coordinate contains the payoff for the first player, while the second coordinate contains the payoff for the second player.

Timing
There are two main ways in which a game can be player (or a turn can be played).

Simoultaneously
Sequentially


For the second case, the extensive form is the most intuitive way to represent a game. For simoultaneous games, the Strategic form is more adequate. Let’s move to this game representation.

title: Introduction:  Incentives Matter

Representing a game
Not all games are worth representing in either one of these two ways. Some games, specially those with continuous action space (so far we saw discrete action spaces) might make the attempt to represent the game futile. We will study these games in the future, but in these cases, we will also be able to use a utility function to find out which strategy would deal the highest expected utility (payoff) for the player.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory
text:
Strategic Form Games
What if we have more than 2 players, and strategies?


If we have \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) players, we will index them: 1,2, \(\dots\), \(N\).
Their strategy space is \(S_i\).
A strategy profile is an ordered tuple \((s_1,s_2,\dots,s_N)\in S_1\times S_2\times\dots S_N\).
\(\pi_i(s_1,\dots,s_N)\) represents the payoff for player \(i\), given the strategy profile \((s_1,s_2,\dots,s_N)\).



We can do better

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory
text:
Strategic Form Games
Given that the strategies of the other players (other than player \(i\)) are out player’s \(i\) control, we will summarize them as \(s_{-i}\). So we will write:
\[\pi_i(s_1,\dots,s_N) = \pi_i(s_i,s_{-i}) \]
And \(s_{-i}\) represents all chosen \(s_j\) when \(j\neq i\). We could say the other’s strategies in the current strategy profile.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory
text:
The Prissoner’s Dilemma
This is a classical game, and this is a great opportunity to introduce it:

Two prissoners, Calvin and Klein, are hauled in for a suspected crime. The \(DA\) speaks to each prisoner separately, and tells them that she more or less has the evidence to convict them but they could make her work a little easier (and help themselves) if they confess to the crime. She offers each of them the following deal: “Confess to the crime, turn a witness for the State, and implicate the ohter guy, and you will do no time. Of course, your confession will be worth a lot less if the other guy confesses as well. I that case, you both go in for 5 years. If you do not confess, however, be aware that we will nail you with the other guy’s confession, and then you will do fifteen years. In the event that I cannot get a confession from either of you, I have enough evidence to put you both away for a year.”


Prajit K. Dutta’s version of this game, in the book Strategies and Games: Theory and Practice. MIT Press, 2001.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory
text:
Equivalence in the Extensive form
We said, these are simoultaneous games, but we do not need that both prissoner’s actually chose simoultaneously. It is enough that when one decide, the other does not know what the first prisoner’s chose.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory
text:
Equivalence in the Extensive form
Think on the Rock-Paper-Scissors game. As both players can see each others hands, simultaneity is necessary.
Suppose now that we introduce a referee. One player tells secretely to the referee what her choice is (rock, paper, or scissors). Then the referee asks the other player, separately what is her own choice. Finally the referee can reveal if there is a winner or a draw. The game works just fine, even though one player played first.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory
text:
Equivalence in the Extensive form
The key was that the player that played last, did not know what the other player played when she made her decision, and also that the first player, knew that they other player was unaware of her move by the time she made her decision.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
Let’s introduce a model to study this problem:

Assume there are only two periods \(t=0,1\).
Player \(i\) in period \(t\) consumes \(c_i^t\) with \(i=1,2\).
Common property resource of size \(y^0>0\).
\(y^1=y^0-\sum_{i\in\{1,2\}} c_i^0\).
If they try to consume more than \(y^t\), in a single period, then each gets \(\frac{y^t}{2}\), and \(y^{t+1}=0\).
Agents drive utility \(u(c)\) from consuming, with \(u'(c)>0\) and \(u''(c)<0\), for example \(u(c)=\ln(c)\).

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
To solve this, we will use a technique that we will revisit in the future with more detailed, which is known Backward Induction. This means we will solve the problem starting from the end:

If there is no \(t=2\), then consumers will try to consume as much as they can in \(t=1\), and therefore \(c_1=c_2=\frac{y^1}{2}\).
Note that \(y^1=y^0-c_1^0-c_2^0\), and therefore \(c_i=\frac{y^0-c_1^0-c_2^0}{2}\) with \(i=1,2\).


Note that \(c_1^1\) and \(c_2^2\) are equal and depend on \(c_1^0\) and \(c_2^0\), and actually these are the only relevant variables. Let’s drop the supra-index for time.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
Let’s solve for consumer 1 (the problem is symmetric). Let’s take \(\bar{c}_2\) as “some” value for \(c_2\).
\[\max_{c_1} \ln(c_1)+\ln\left(\frac{y-c_1-\bar{c}_2}{2}\right)\]
From where deriving first order conditions we obtain:
\[\frac{1}{c_1}-\frac{1}{y-c_1-\bar{c}_2}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad c_1=\frac{y-\bar{c}_2}{2}\]

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
What we have here is, that if player 2 choses to consume \(\bar{c}_2\) in the first period, then player 1 will chose to consume \(\frac{y-\bar{c}_2}{2}\). Because the problem is symmetric, if we repeat the exercise, but now from the point of view of player 2, we will get \[c_2=\frac{y-\bar{c}_1}{2}\]
These are the best response functions of players 1 and 2. We know that both players should be best responding at the same time in a Nash Equilibrium.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
We get the following system of equations:
\[c_1^*=\frac{y-c_2^*}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad c_2^*=\frac{y-c_1^*}{2}\]
For example
\[c_1^*=\frac{y-\frac{y-c_1^*}{2}}{2}=\frac{y}{4}+\frac{c_1^*}{4}\ \Rightarrow\ c_1^*=\frac{y}{3}\]
By symmetry, \(c_2^*=\frac{y}{3}\).

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
What we have then, is that both consumers will consume \(\frac{y}{3}\) in the first period and \(\frac{y}{6}\) in the second period. Their lifetime utility will be \(\ln \left(\frac{y}{3}\right)+\ln\left(\frac{y}{6}\right)=\ln\left(\frac{y^2}{18}\right)\). This is a Nash Equilibrium, because both players are best-responding.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
Is this socially optimal?






Social Optimum


A pattern of consumption, \((\hat{c}_1,\hat{c}_2)\) is socially optimal if it maximizes the sum of the two player’s utility, that is, if it solves the following problem:
\[\max_{c_1,c_2} \ln (c_1) + \ln (c_2) + 2 \ln \left(\frac{y-(c_1+c_2)}{2}\right)\]

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
This leads to the first order conditions:
\[\frac{1}{c_1^*}-\frac{2}{y-c_1^*-c_2^*}=0\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{1}{c_2^*}-\frac{2}{y-c_1^*-c_2^*}=0\]
And solutions \(c_1^*=c_2^*=c^*\), and replacing in either equation, we obtain \(c^*=\frac{y}{4}\). Lifetime utility is \[2\ln \left(\frac{y}{4}\right)=\ln\left(\frac{y^2}{16}\right)>\ln\left(\frac{y^2}{18}\right)\]

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory I
text:
The tragedy of the Commons
We can see the The tragedy of the Commons in action, the Nash Equilibrium leads to overconsumption in the first period and therefore to a lower level of lifetime utility.
Note:

If player 1, for example, would try to cut consumption in the first period to “save” for the future,
player 2 would consume now half more (look at the BRF),
and in the second period, consumer 1 would have to split the savings (just half of his consumption reduction) with player 2.

Extensive Representation of a Game
We have a somehow informal definition of the extensive games, let’s formalize it. There are three consistency requirements:

Single starting point
No Cycles
One way to Proceed



It is important to know where the game starts, and so there must be one, and only one, starting point. Hence, a situation as two games in parallel is unacceptable.
It is important that we not hit an impasse while playing the game; it must not be possible for the branches of a tree ot double back and create a cycle.
It is important tha there be no ambiguity about how a game proceeds, and so there must not be two or more branches leading to a node.

Definition


The predecessors of a node, say \(\alpha\), are those nodes from which you can go (through a sequence of branches) to \(\alpha\).

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory II
text:
Extensive Representation of a Game
The three consisntey requirements can be defined using the definition of a predecessor:


A node cannot be a predecessor to itself.
A predecessor’s predecessor is also a predecessor: if a node \(\beta\) is a predecessor of \(\alpha\), and a node \(\gamma\) is, in turn, a predecessor of \(\beta\), then \(\gamma\) is a predecessor of \(\alpha\) as well.
Predecessors can be ranked: if \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) are both predecessors of \(\alpha\), it must be the case that either \(\beta\) is a predecessor of \(\gamma\) or vice-versa.
There must be a common predecessor: Consider any two nodes, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), neither of which precedes the other. Then there must be a node \(\gamma\) that is the predecessor of both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

Kuhn’s (and Zermelo’s) Theorem


Every game of perfect information with a finite number of nodes has a solution to backward induction. Indeed, if for every player it is the case that no two payoffs are the same, then there is a unique solution to backward induction.




The proof is very simple, and it is, by coincidence, a proof by induction:1

Show that for \(n=1\), where \(n\) is the number of “steps” of the game, the game is solved by finding the best alternative for the playing player.

Repeated Games






Definition


A repeated game is defined by a stage game \(G\) and the number of its repetitions, say \(T\). The stage game \(G\) is a game in strategic form: \(G=\{S_i,\pi_i ; i=1,\dots,N\}\) where \(S_i\) is player \(i's\) set of strategies and \(\pi_i\) is his payoff function [and it depends on \((s_1,s_2,\dots,N)\)].

If \(T<\infty\), the game is called finitely repeated game,
If \(T=\infty\), the game is called infinitely repeated game.

text:
Examples


The “Lame Duck” Period in Politics: Elected officials might cooperate at the beginning of their term to gain favor and pass legislation with the support for future bills. If there is no re-election, in the latest months the officials might try to pass controversial bills and pardons.
Military Occupations and withdrawal date: Locals that have to decide to support occupying force or insurgents, the value of supporting occupying forces vanishes at the departure date.
Short-term Humanitarian Interventions: Local contractors provide service for payment for NGOs.

title: Fundamentals of  Game Theory II

Corollary


In any finitely repeated game, one SPNE of the repeated game is for players to play a one-stage NE over and over again.










Proposition


Consider a finitely repeated game \((G,T)\) with \(G=\{S_i,\pi_i ; i=1,\dots,N\}\). Suppose the stage game \(G\) has exactly one NE, say \(s^*=(s_1^*,s_2^*,\dots,s_N^*)\). Then the repeated game has a unique SPNE. In this equilibrium, player \(i\) plays \(s_i^*\) at every one of the \(T\) stages, regardless of what might have been played, by her or any of the others, in any previous stage.

In the last stage, surely \(s^*\) will be played, as is the \(NE\) for a single NE of the game.
In the stage before, the payoffs are determined, as in the next stage, whatever is decided, \(s^*\) will be played in the next stage, so this will be traeted as an independent stage, and then \(s^*\) will be played as well.
Iterate, and you find that \(s^*\) is played in every stage of the game.

It is trivial to show that if \(|\pi_{it}|<\infty\) \(\forall t\), then this sum is finite.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Moral Hazard






Definition


Moral Hazard is a term that refers to the situation when an person acts when she does not bear the full (good or bad) consequences of her acts.



For example if you own a 🚗, and if you crash it, you will have to pay all the costs with fixing it 🔧.
Now, if you have insurance, these costs pass along to the insurer. It is expected that you would drive less carefully than without insurance.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Moral Hazard
The true cause of the problem is that the Insurance Company cannot know, at every moment, how are you driving. Of course there are some things that are present in the contract:

They will not pay if you were speeding.
They will not pay if you were driving under the influence of drugs.
etc.

But there are a plethora of irresponsible behavior that the company cannot monitor.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Moral Hazard
In this case, the person who has to act and has private information on his actions, is known as the agent, while who is bearing the consequences of the actions of the agent is called the principal.
At the core this is a problem of missaligned incentives: what is good for the agent, might not be necessarily good for the principal.

title: Moral Hazard in Public Finance
text:
This model is taken almost literaly from Principled Agents? The Political Economy of Good Government from Timothy Besley, Chapter 4.
There are two periods. In each period \(t\), the government must decide on three things. The level of valuable public spending \(G_t\), the value of public spending devoted to private ends \(s_t\), and the level of taxation \(x_t\). Let \(x_t\in[0,X]\) so taxation level is bounded.
In each period, the unit cost of providing a public good is \(\theta_t\), determined randomly by nature. The cost of the public good is i.i.d, represented by \(\theta\in\{L,H\}\) with \(L<H\) and \(Pr(\theta_t=H)=q\).
For now, assume that Government Budget is balanced (nor deficit allowed, nor surplus). The budget constraint each period is:
\[x_t=\theta_t G_t+ s_t\]
Welfare of the voter is defined as \(W(G,x)=G-\mu C(x)\), where \(C(\cdot)\) is increasing and strictly convex function, and \(\mu\) is a scalar that weights the cost of public funds.


What would be the optimal levels of taxing and spending for a benevolent government (i.e. that only cares about voter’s welfare)? This of course means \(s_t=0\) \(t=1,2\). Let’s define
\[G_{\theta}^*(\mu)=\arg \max \{G-\mu C(\theta G)\}\]
And let \(x_{\theta}^*=\theta G_{\theta}^*\) with \(W^g(\theta,\mu)\) being the level of voter welfare at these optimal levels. Finally, let
\[E[W^g(\mu)]=q W^g(H,\mu)+(1-q)W^g(L,\mu)\]
Note that \(C(\cdot)\) being strictly convex, implies that the government is optimally larger when the cost of public goods is lower, and therefore \(x_L^*>x_H^*\)






TipSide note



Note that the first order condition on \(G-\mu C(\theta G)\) leads to
\[\frac{1}{\mu}=\frac{\partial C}{\partial G}(\theta G) \times \theta\]
To preserve the equality, a lower value of \(\theta\) requires a larger value of the derivative. This derivative is increasing (strict convexity of \(C\) ensures this), and note that \(\theta\) inside the argument is also smaller, and therefore \(G\) must increase to compensate. This will require a larger government, but this compensation shall be large enough to compensate the decrease in \(\theta\) inside the argument, and also the decrease in the \(\theta\) multiplying outside of the derivative! Then the argument inside must be larger than in case we have a larger value of \(\theta\).


We further assume that \(X>x_L^*\). Further, from teh welfare function, it is clear that lower levels of \(\mu\) are better, and moreover, \(G^*_\theta\) is also increasing for lower values of \(\mu\). The less costly is to fund the public goods, the more public goods are better for the voters.

title: Moral Hazard in Public Finance
text:
Politics
Consider two time periods, \(t=1,2\). Between periods there is an election, where the voters might decide between the incumbent and a challenger.
The cost shock \(\theta\), and the amount of rent diverted for private purposes, \(s\), is privately observed by the polititian. On the other hand, \(G\) and \(x\) are observable by voters. Voters can discipline the polititian with their vote. If they want to punish the incumbent, they vote for the challenger, and they can reward the incumbent by renewing the mandate. They will punish/reward the incumbent to make them behave closer to what voters would like, to minimize rent diversion.
We consider a game where voters can announce (and commit to) an incentive based re-election rule prior to the incumbent’s first period policy being chosen. Let the re-election rule used by voters be denoted by a function \(\sigma(G,x)\). Then for fixed \(G\), the incumbent’s rent extraction problem is to choose rent diversion in Periods 1 and 2 denoted by \((s_1,s_2)\) to maximize \(s_1+\beta\sigma(G,\theta G+s_1)s_2\).
In period 2, there are no re-election incentives to restraint rentseeking, and every polititian will choose \(s_2=X\). In period 1, the incumbent can be rewarded for reducing his/her rent-seeking. Voters reason as follows: since incumbents can always extract \(X\) today and forego re-election, then they must be offered an incentive to prevent them from doing so. Since all they care about are rents, they are indifferent between all packages which yield them \(X\). Hence, consider the threshold level of rent \(\hat{s}(\sigma)\), whcih satisfies:
\[\hat{s}(\sigma)+\sigma\beta X=X\]
As long as the level of permissible rent satisfies this, the incumbent will choose \(\hat{s}(\sigma)\) adn get re-elected with probability \(\sigma\). However, since the level of Period 1 rent-seeking that satisfies this incentive constraint is decreasing in \(\sigma\), ti is best for voters to set \(\sigma=1\). In the languange of the P-A literature, wemay therefore think of the condition \(s_1\geq (1-\beta)X\) as the participation constraint that must be satisfied to ensure that the incumbent produces the level of public spending desired by voters for each cost level \(\theta=L,H\).
The pure Moral Hazard model is consistent with a term limit effect in polititians’ choices of the kind found by Besley and Case (1995b). However, given the choice in reality between a challenger who can serve an extra term in office and an incumbent who will be a lame duck, the model cannot explain why the voters would ever prefer a lame duck.
The model predicts that rent taking is lower by \(\beta X\) when polititians face re-election incentives. The more patient are polititians, the larger the rent improvement for voters. The level of public spending is higher in the first period than the second and the level of taxation is \(X\) in Period 2 and less than \(X\) in Period 1.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Moral Hazard
What to do then?
Principals have to design schemes that incentive the agent to behave more in line with the Principal’s goals. Of course, these incentives are costly.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Suppose the following alternative setup:

\(e\) is effort exherted by the Agent, with cost \(c(e)=\frac{e^2}{2}\).
Let \(x(e)=x\cdot e\) the return expected for the Principal.
Suppose the contract is based on a compensation \(w(x)=a+bx\). Note that \(b\leq 1\), otherwise the Principal loses money, it would be giving away everything and then some.
Suppose the Agent can get utility \(\underline{u}\) in an alternative job.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Let:

both agent and principal be risk neutral: \(u_a(w)=w\), and \(u_p(\pi)=\pi\).
the outcome be \(x\in\{0,\xi\}\).
effort be chosen as \(e\in[0,1]\), and \(Pr(x=\xi|e)=e\).
the wage have fixed \(a\) pay and bonus \(b\), paid in case \(x=\xi\).
Let \(c(e)=\frac{e^2}{2}\) be the cost of effort.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
The maximization problem of the principal is given by:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{e,a,b}\quad &-a+e(\xi-b)\\
  s.t.\quad &a+eb-c(e)\geq\bar{u}\\
  &e\in\arg\max_{\hat{e}}\{a+\hat{e}b-c(\hat{e})\}\\
  &a\geq -w
\end{aligned}
\]
Let’s assume, further, than \(\omega = 0\), i.e. we will not allow negative fixed wage (or transfers from the agent to the principal). This is know as limited liability or cash constraint.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Grossman and Hart (1983) show that under some conditions (satisfied in this model and in most of the simple versions of this model) the problem can be solved in two stages:

Solve the problem for the agent, taking everything external to the agent as a parameter.
Solve the problem of the principal, substituting the solution of the agent as a function of the principal’s variables.

This is how we will proceed.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Given \(a\) and \(b\), the agent will maximize her utility, so computing the FOC we get:
\[b-c'=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=e^*\]
So the agent will choose optimally \(e=b\).

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
The problem for the principal is now:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{a,e}\quad &-a+e(\xi-e)\\
  s.t.\quad &a+e^2-\frac{e^2}{2}\geq\bar{u}\\
  &a\geq 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Now, if \(e^*=0\), the agent will accept to participate if and only if \(a\geq \bar{u}\). For simplicity assume \(\bar{u}=0\).

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{a,e}\quad &-a+e(\xi-e)\\
  s.t.\quad &a+\frac{e^2}{2}\geq0\\
  &a\geq 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Which constraint is irrelevant now?

The Participation Constraint, as \(\frac{e^2}{2}\geq 0\). Then the optimal is \(a=0\). Now what is the optimal level of effort?

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{e}\quad &e(\xi-e)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
And from there \(e^*=\frac{\xi}{2}\). Note that this makes \(b=\frac{\xi}{2}\). So the expected payoffs are:

\(E[u_a]=0+\left(\frac{\xi}{2}\right)^2-\frac{\xi^2}{8}=\frac{\xi^2}{8}\)
\(E[u_p]=-0+\frac{\xi}{2}\left(\xi-\frac{\xi}{2}\right)=\frac{\xi^2}{4}\)

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
What if the Principal could observe effort?
Then the Incentive Compatibility is unnecessary, and the principal needs just to compensate effort (non probabilistically)
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{e}\quad &e\xi-c(e)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
Which has solution \(e^*=\xi\), \(a=0\), and \(b=c(\xi)=\frac{\xi^2}{2}\). The expected utility of the agent is \(0\), and the expected profit for the principal is \(\frac{\xi^2}{2}\).

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Some notes:

With information asymmetry, the agent can extract information rents from the principal, at the cost of a worse outcome overall.
Without information asymmetry, the principal can extrat the whole surplus, which is larger than the case with information asymmetries.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
In general,

Incentivizing hard work is costly.
The higher the profits, the larger the bonus.
The principal is almost always worse off in the presence of moral hazard, while the agent might be better off.

Suppose the following alternative setup:

\(e\) is effort exherted by the Agent, with cost \(c(e)=\frac{e^2}{2}\).
Let \(x(e)=x\cdot e\) the return expected for the Principal.
Suppose the contract is based on a compensation \(w(x)=a+bx\). Note that \(b\leq 1\), otherwise the Principal loses money, it would be giving away everything and then some.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model

In the first case, the Principal bears all the risk (fixed wage, whatever happens).
In the second case, the Agent bears all the risk (fixed \(f\), whatever happens).


The most common scenario is an intermediate situation, a base wage plus a bonus that depends on the outcome.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
What is sure, is that the agent will choose \(e_h\) over \(e_l\) only if it is convenient to her, i.e. the expected utility of that choice is larger than the expected utility of the alternative.

\[
\begin{aligned}
  E[u|e_h] &\geq E[u|e_l]\\
  0.6 u(w_g)+0.1 u(w_b)-d_h &\geq 0.1 u(w_g)+0.6 u(w_b)-d_l\\
  \frac{1}{2}\left[u(w_g)-u(w_b)\right] &\geq d_h-d_l
\end{aligned}\]

Before continuing, let’s think on the case without Moral Hazard (without hidden information), to have as a benchmark.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Suppose effort is observable, then the Principal could offer compensation based on effort instead of the outcome, \(w_H\) when \(e_H\) is observed, and \(w_L\) when \(e_L\) is observed. To incentivize high effort it would be enough that:
\[u(w_H)-d_H\geq u(w_L)-d_L\]
But, is incetivizing high effort convenient for the Principal?

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
Conditional on effort the principal gets:

For \(e_H\), the profits are \(0.6g+0.3m+0.1b-w_H\)
For \(e_L\), the profits are \(0.1g+0.3m+0.6b-w_L\)


It is easy to check that \(e_H\) is convenient for the principal if and only if
\[\frac{1}{2}[g-b]\geq W_H-W_L\]

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
A Principal-Agent model
More generically, the principal needs to solve:

\[
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{e, w}\quad &E[\pi|e]\\
  s.t.\quad E[u|e]&\geq \bar{u} \\
            e &\in \arg \max_{\hat{e}} E[u|\hat{e}]
\end{aligned}
\]

text:

An Example:
Let \(u(w)=2\sqrt{w}\), \(d_H=10\), \(d_L=0\), and profits levels are \(g=200\), \(m=100\), \(b=50\).
We have for the agent then:

\(E[u|e_h]=1.2\sqrt{w_g}+0.6 \sqrt{w_m}+0.2\sqrt{w_b}-10\)
\(E[u|e_l]=0.2 \sqrt{w_g}+0.6 \sqrt{w_m}+1.2\sqrt{w_b}-0\)

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Bayesian Games Framework

A Bayesian game consists of:

Set of players \(N = \{1, 2, ..., n\}\)
Type spaces \(T_i\) for each player \(i\)
Prior beliefs \(p(t)\) over type profiles
Action spaces \(A_i\) for each player
Payoff functions \(u_i(a, t)\) depending on actions and types

Players maximize expected utility given beliefs about opponents’ types

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 1: Entry Deterrence Game
Incumbent faces potential entrant with unknown costs:

Entrant can be high-cost type (probability \(p\)) or low-cost type (probability \(1-p\))
Entrant decides: Enter or Stay Out
Incumbent decides: Fight or Accommodate

Payoffs depend on entrant’s type, which incumbent doesn’t observe

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Entry Deterrence Payoffs
If entrant is high-cost type: - Enter + Fight: \((-1, 0)\) - Enter + Accommodate: \((1, 1)\) - Stay Out: \((0, 2)\)
If entrant is low-cost type: - Enter + Fight: \((0, 0)\) - Enter + Accommodate: \((2, 1)\) - Stay Out: \((0, 2)\)
Incumbent must form beliefs about entrant’s type

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
A strategy profile where each player’s strategy is optimal given:

Their beliefs about other players’ types
The strategies of other players

Formally: \(s_i^*(t_i) \in \arg\max_{a_i} \sum_{t_{-i}} p(t_{-i}|t_i) u_i(a_i, s_{-i}^*(t_{-i}), t_i, t_{-i})\)
Each type of each player best responds to opponents’ strategies in expected utility

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 2: Sealed-Bid Auction
First-price sealed-bid auction with incomplete information:

\(n\) bidders with private valuations \(v_i\)
Valuations drawn independently from \([0, 1]\) with distribution \(F\)
Each bidder submits sealed bid \(b_i\)
Highest bidder wins and pays their bid
Payoff to winner: \(v_i - b_i\), losers get 0

Must find equilibrium bidding strategies

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Auction Equilibrium Strategy
With symmetric independent private values and uniform distribution:
Equilibrium bidding strategy: \(b(v) = \frac{n-1}{n}v\)
Intuition: - Bidding your true value yields zero expected profit - Must shade bid below valuation - Trade-off between winning probability and profit conditional on winning - With more bidders, less shading needed

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 3: Cournot Competition with Uncertainty
Two firms choose quantities simultaneously:

Firm 1 has cost \(c_1\) (known to both)
Firm 2’s cost \(c_2\) is private: either \(c_L\) with probability \(q\) or \(c_H\) with probability \(1-q\)
Inverse demand: \(P(Q) = a - Q\) where \(Q = q_1 + q_2\)

Firm 1 must maximize expected profit over Firm 2’s possible types

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Cournot Equilibrium with Incomplete Information
Firm 2’s strategies: \(q_2(c_L)\) and \(q_2(c_H)\)
Firm 1’s best response: \(q_1^* = \frac{a - c_1 - q \cdot q_2(c_L) - (1-q) \cdot q_2(c_H)}{2}\)
Low-cost Firm 2: \(q_2(c_L) = \frac{a - 2c_L + c_1}{3}\)
High-cost Firm 2: \(q_2(c_H) = \frac{a - 2c_H + c_1}{3}\)
Expected quantity from Firm 2 enters Firm 1’s calculation

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Application: Insurance Markets
Adverse selection in insurance:

Individuals have private information about risk type
High-risk types (probability \(p_H\) of accident)
Low-risk types (probability \(p_L\) of accident)
Insurer cannot distinguish types

Result: Pooling or separating equilibria depending on cost structure

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Insurance Market Equilibrium
Separating equilibrium conditions:

High-risk types buy full insurance at actuarially fair price
Low-risk types buy partial insurance
Each type’s contract maximizes utility subject to zero-profit constraint
No cross-subsidization between types

Self-selection: contract design induces types to reveal information

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 4: The Market for Lemons
Used car market (Akerlof 1970):

Sellers know car quality \(q \in [0, 1]\)
Buyers only know distribution of qualities
Buyer willing to pay expected value
Seller willing to sell if price exceeds \(q\)

Can lead to market unraveling when asymmetry is severe

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Lemons Equilibrium
If buyers believe average quality is \(\bar{q}\):

Willing to pay \(\bar{q}\)
Only sellers with \(q \leq \bar{q}\) will sell
Actual average quality is \(\bar{q}/2\)
Buyers revise beliefs downward

Unraveling continues until only lowest quality items trade or market collapses entirely

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Signaling Games
Dynamic games where informed player moves first:

Nature chooses sender’s type
Sender observes type, chooses signal/action
Receiver observes signal (not type), chooses response
Payoffs depend on type, signal, and response

Education as signal of ability is classic example

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 5: Job Market Signaling
Workers have high or low ability (private information):

High ability: fraction \(\lambda\), productivity \(\theta_H\)
Low ability: fraction \(1-\lambda\), productivity \(\theta_L\)
Workers choose education level \(e\) at cost \(c(e, \theta)\)
Cost assumption: \(c_\theta < 0\) (education cheaper for high ability)
Firms observe education, offer wage

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Separating Equilibrium in Signaling
High-ability workers choose \(e^*\), low-ability choose \(e = 0\)
Firms’ beliefs: \(e \geq e^*\) implies high ability, \(e < e^*\) implies low ability
Wages: \(w(e \geq e^*) = \theta_H\), \(w(e < e^*) = \theta_L\)
Incentive compatibility requires: - \(\theta_H - c(e^*, \theta_H) \geq \theta_L\) - \(\theta_L \geq \theta_H - c(e^*, \theta_L)\)

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
Refinement for dynamic games with incomplete information:
Requirements: 1. Sequential rationality: strategies optimal at every information set 2. Belief consistency: beliefs derived from Bayes’ rule wherever possible 3. Off-path beliefs: must be specified even for unreached information sets
Eliminates non-credible equilibria in signaling games

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 6: Poker (Simplified)
Two-player poker with incomplete information:

Player 1 receives high or low card (equally likely)
Player 1: Bet or Fold
Player 2 (if P1 bets): Call or Fold
Bluffing: betting with low card
Calling: responding to potential bluff

Mixed strategies emerge in equilibrium

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Poker Equilibrium
Player 1 strategy: - Always bet with high card - Bluff (bet with low card) with probability \(b\)
Player 2 strategy: - Call with probability \(c\)
Equilibrium values of \(b\) and \(c\) make opponents indifferent, preventing exploitation

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design

So far we have studied what players will do, given a set of rules and payoffs (not entirely true, i.e. Contracts)
Mechanism Design asks, if I want a specific outcome:

What de rules must be?
Is it even possible?



Basically now we design the game to induce the players to play in a specific manner.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 7: Vickrey Auction
Second-price sealed-bid auction:

Highest bidder wins
Winner pays second-highest bid
Dominant strategy: bid true valuation

Truth-telling is optimal regardless of others’ bids: - If you win, you pay less than your value - If you lose by bidding truthfully, overbidding wouldn’t help

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Application: Spectrum Auctions
FCC spectrum auctions combine incomplete information elements:

Bidders have private valuations for licenses
May have synergies across licenses
Common value components (resale value)
Strategic interaction across multiple items

Simultaneous ascending auction design addresses these features

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Common Value vs. Private Value
Private values: \(v_i\) independent across bidders
Common values: true value \(v\) same for all, but each has private signal \(s_i\)
Winner’s curse in common value auctions: - Winning means you had highest signal - Conditional on winning, true value likely lower than your estimate - Rational bidders shade bids to account for this

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 8: Oil Lease Auctions
Drilling rights with uncertain reserves:

True value \(v\) unknown to all bidders
Each has private geological survey \(s_i\)
Surveys correlated with true value
Winner likely overestimated value

Equilibrium involves bidding below signal value to avoid winner’s curse

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Screening
Principal designs menu to separate agent types:

Insurance company offers coverage options
Monopolist offers quality-quantity bundles
Employer offers compensation packages

Second-degree price discrimination exploits self-selection

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 9: Monopoly Price Discrimination
Monopolist faces high and low-value consumers:
Cannot observe type directly, so offers two options: - High quantity at high price (for high types) - Low quantity at low price (for low types)
Design satisfies incentive compatibility: each type prefers their intended option

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Reputation and Incomplete Information
Reputation as repeated game with incomplete information:

Long-run player may be “commitment type” or “rational type”
Short-run players uncertain about long-run player’s type
Rational type can mimic commitment type to build reputation
Reputation effects create incentives even for rational types

Chain store paradox resolution

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 10: Chain Store Game
Chain store faces sequential entry in \(n\) markets:

In each market, potential entrant decides whether to enter
If entry occurs, chain chooses Fight or Accommodate
Small probability chain is “tough type” that always fights

Even rational chain fights early entrants to build reputation of toughness

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Cheap Talk
Communication without direct payoff consequences:

Sender has private information
Sends costless message to receiver

Receiver takes action affecting both parties
Messages are “cheap talk” if they don’t directly affect payoffs

Can communication be informative in equilibrium?

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 11: Expert Advice
Expert knows true state, advises decision-maker:

States: \(\theta \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}\)
Expert prefers action slightly above true state
Decision-maker prefers action equal to true state
Expert sends message, decision-maker chooses action

Partitional equilibria: expert reveals interval containing state

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Partitional Equilibria in Cheap Talk
With preference misalignment parameter \(b\):
Number of informative intervals in equilibrium bounded by \(1/(4b)\)
Greater conflict of interest means less information transmitted: - Small \(b\): many intervals, precise communication - Large \(b\): few intervals, coarse communication - Perfect alignment \((b=0)\): full revelation possible

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Forward Induction
Refinement based on rationality of past actions:

If player made choice that seems suboptimal under some beliefs
Update beliefs: player wouldn’t have chosen that unless it was optimal
Requires that player had good reason for observed action

Strengthens PBE by restricting off-path beliefs

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 12: Beer-Quiche Game
Morning routine reveals information:

Two types: Tough (prob 0.9) or Weak (prob 0.1)
Tough prefers beer, Weak prefers quiche
After breakfast, may face challenge
Challenger fights if believes opponent is Weak

Pooling on beer can signal toughness, but forward induction refines

text:
Applications in Industrial Organization
Incomplete information models explain:

Entry deterrence through limit pricing
Predatory pricing to signal costs
Patent races with uncertain R&D costs
Merger decisions with private valuations
Quality signaling through warranties

Key insight: information asymmetries drive strategic behavior

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Contract Theory Applications
Incomplete information in principal-agent relationships:

Employer cannot observe worker ability or effort
Lender uncertain about borrower risk
Regulator doesn’t know firm’s costs

Optimal contracts trade off rent extraction and efficiency: - Information rents to higher types - Distortions for lower types

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Experimental Evidence
Laboratory experiments test predictions:

Overbidding in first-price auctions relative to theory
Winner’s curse observed in common-value auctions
Signaling games: partial pooling occurs
Trust games: incomplete information reduces cooperation

Behavioral factors matter but basic insights hold

Computational Considerations
Finding equilibria in incomplete information games:

First-order conditions for continuum types
Fixed-point algorithms for discrete types
Numerical integration for expected payoffs
Monte Carlo methods for complex type spaces

Tractability varies with type space dimensionality

Bayesian Nash equilibrium incorporates beliefs

Applications across economics and beyond

Example 2: Pure Strategies

Suppose \(H\) plays \(F\) for sure.
In this case, \(W\) will play \(FS\).


But can this be an equilibrium?


If so, H must stick with \(F\), \(i.e.\) \(F\) must be a best response to W strategy’s \(FS\).

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 2: Pure Strategies

Remember, H expects W to be type 1 with probability \(p\), so her expected payoffs are:

\(E[\pi_H(F,FS)]=p3+(1-p)0=3p\)
\(E[\pi_H(S,FS)]=p0+(1-p)1=1-p\)

If H is to stick with \(F\) when W is playing \(FS\), then it must be true that:
\[3p\geq 1-p\ \Rightarrow\ p\geq \frac{1}{4}\]

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 2: Pure Strategies

Suppose now that H plays \(S\) for sure.
In this case, W will play \(SF\).

But can this be an equilibrium? If so, H must stick with \(S\), \(i.e.\) \(S\) must be a best response to W strategy’s \(SF\).

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 2: Pure Strategies

Remember, H expects W to be type 1 with probability \(p\), so her expected payoffs are:

\(E[\pi_H(F,SF)]=p0+(1-p)3=3(1-p)\)
\(E[\pi_H(S,SF)]=p1+(1-p)0=p\)

If H is to stick with \(S\) when W is playing \(SF\), then it must be true that:
\[3(1-p)\leq p\ \Rightarrow\ p\geq \frac{3}{4}\]

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Example 2: Pure Strategies
Conclusion:

If \(p\geq \frac{3}{4}\) there are 2 BNEs, \((F,FS)\) and \((S,SF)\).
If \(\frac{1}{4}\leq p < \frac{3}{4}\) there is only 1 BNE, \((F,FS)\).
If \(p<\frac{1}{4}\) there is no BNE in pure strategies.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design
In general, the set of players is something that will be given, i.e. is something we cannot design, but the designer can choose:

choices available to players
payoffs

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design
However, there are some constraints for the designer

There cannot be any coercion (why would you need to incentivize behavior if you can force it)
Players can choose to not participate, and therefore the game must give enough incentives to make players want to play.

The optimal design is a mechanism whose equilibrium is the one that generates the highest payoff for the designer.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design
More formally:



Definition


A mechanism is a game (a set of rules) that specifies the strategies that the player can choose from and the outcome for every choice.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design

Let a strategy for a player \(s\).
Let the outcome of a game be denoted by \(t\).
Let the type of the player be denoted by \(\theta\).
Let the payoff of the player be represented by the function \(\pi(s,t,\theta)\).

The designer can choose \(s\) and \(t\), but \(\theta\) and \(\pi\) is out of his control.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Auctions
Auctions are, probably, the most transparent mechanism.

Auctioneer does not know the player’s individual valuations.
Auctioneer wants to exert as much money as she can from bidders.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design



Definition


Suppose there are two types \(\theta\) and \(\mu\). The designer assigns \((s_{\theta},t_{\theta})\) as strategies and outcomes for the player type \(\theta\), and \((s_{\mu},t_{\mu})\) for the player type \(\mu\).
A design is said to be incentive compatible if:
\[\pi(s_{\theta},t_{\theta},\theta)\geq \pi(s,t,\theta)\quad \forall s,\ \forall t\] and \[\pi(s_{\mu},t_{\mu},\mu)\geq \pi(s,t,\mu)\quad \forall s,\ \forall t\]



This is, every player has incentives to tell the truth.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design



Definition


Suppose there are two types \(\theta\) and \(\mu\), with reservation utility \(\underline{\pi}_{\theta}\) and \(\underline{\pi}_{\mu}\).
A design is said to be idividually rational if:
\[\pi(s_{\theta},t_{\theta},\theta)\geq \underline{\pi}_\theta\] and \[\pi(s_{\mu},t_{\mu},\mu)\geq \underline{\pi}_\mu\]



This is, every player has incentives to participate.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design
Without much surprise we call the designer the Principal.
Any design the Principal devices to maximize her expected payoff must be incentive compatible and individually rational. Her payoff usually depends on the strategies chosen by the players.
For surprise to none, there as infinite number of ways in which a Principal can set a mechanism, however we will focus on the class named direct-revelation mechanisms.

title: Games under  Asymmetric Information
text:
Mechanism Design
Direct-revelation mechanism:

Each player is free to lie about his type. \(\theta\) can claim to be \(\mu\) if so desires, and vice-versa.
Suppose that if you claim to be type \(\theta\), the mechanism assings you \((s_\theta,t_\theta)\), and \((s_\mu,t_\mu)\) for the \(\mu\) type
